# 🛰️ First Satellite vs. Latest Satellite (2026)

---

## 🚀 SPUTNIK 1 — The First Satellite (1957)

Sputnik 1 was the **first artificial Earth satellite**, launched into an elliptical low Earth orbit by the **Soviet Union on October 4, 1957**.

### Size & Weight
It was only about the size of a beach ball — **22.8 inches (58 cm) in diameter** — and weighed just **183.9 pounds (83.6 kg)**.

### Shape & Design
It was an extremely simple satellite — a **metal sphere** with four long antennas protruding from it. It contained a **thermometer, a fan, a radio transmitter, batteries, and little else**.

### Orbit
Sputnik 1's orbit was elliptical; it was approximately **230 km from Earth at its closest point** (perigee) and **940 km away at its furthest point** (apogee). It took just under **an hour and a half to circle the entire planet**.

### Mission & Purpose
The only cargo onboard Sputnik was a **low-power radio transmitter**, which broadcast a beeping noise at regular intervals — a signal that could be heard by radio listeners around the world.

### Lifespan
The satellite transmitters operated for **three weeks**, until the on-board chemical batteries failed. The orbit then decayed **92 days after launch (January 4, 1958)**, after completing about **1,400 orbits** of the Earth.

### Historical Impact
The Sputnik launch **marked the start of the space age** and the US-USSR space race, and led to the **creation of NASA**.

---

## 🌐 ViaSat-3 F3 — One of the Latest Satellites (2026)

SpaceX launched the **ViaSat-3 F3** satellite to complete Viasat's trio of high-capacity **Geostationary Orbit (GEO)** satellites, lifting off on a **Falcon Heavy** from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida.

### Platform & Builder
Built on **Boeing's high-power 702MP+ platform** and integrated at Boeing's El Segundo facility in California, VS-3 F3 delivers state-of-the-art technology to maximize efficient, flexible bandwidth deployment.

### Capacity & Technology
Designed to deliver **over 1 Terabit per second (Tbps) of throughput capacity**, the satellite leverages innovative payload design and **advanced beam-forming technology** to optimize and steer immense capacity in real time.

### Mission & Purpose
The satellite is intended to provide **broadband connectivity** with speeds of **100+ megabits per second** to homes, businesses, aircraft, government and defense markets, and maritime enterprises across the **Asia-Pacific** region.

### Orbit Type
The Falcon Heavy launch delivered the satellite to a favorable transfer orbit, where its **electric propulsion** took over to place ViaSat-3 F3 into **geostationary orbit**.

### Service Entry
The satellite is expected to **enter service by late summer 2026**.

---

## 📊 Side-by-Side Comparison

| Feature | **Sputnik 1 (1957)** | **ViaSat-3 F3 (2026)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Launch Date** | October 4, 1957 | April 27, 2026 |
| **Launched By** | Soviet Union | Viasat (USA) via SpaceX |
| **Launch Vehicle** | Modified R-7 Rocket | SpaceX Falcon Heavy |
| **Mass** | 83.6 kg (184 lbs) | Several thousand kg |
| **Size** | 58 cm sphere (beach ball) | Large geostationary platform |
| **Orbit Type** | Low Earth Orbit (LEO) | Geostationary Orbit (GEO) |
| **Altitude** | ~230–940 km | ~35,786 km |
| **Payload** | Radio transmitter & thermometer | 1+ Tbps broadband communications |
| **Technology** | Batteries, simple antennas | Advanced beam-forming, electric propulsion |
| **Lifespan** | ~3 weeks (transmitting), 92 days (orbital) | Designed for ~15–20 years |
| **Purpose** | Prove satellite orbit was possible | Global high-speed internet & defense comms |
| **Impact** | Started the Space Race & creation of NASA | Completes global broadband coverage |

---

The contrast is staggering — in less than 70 years, humanity went from a **beach ball-sized beeping sphere** to a **terabit-per-second internet satellite** the size of a bus, orbiting 60× higher and serving millions of users worldwide! 🌍
